Penicillin. The first widely used antibiotic, a compound derived from the mold Penicillium notatum that revolutionized medicine by enabling the treatment of bacterial infections. Discovered accidentally by Alexander Fleming in 1928, its development and mass production during World War II saved countless lives. Penicillin remains one of the most significant pharmaceutical discoveries in human history.

Fleming discovered it when he noticed that a mold contaminating a bacterial culture had killed surrounding bacteria, a serendipitous observation that launched modern antibiotic research. He initially named the active compound "mold juice" before developing the name penicillin. It works by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis, causing the cell wall to rupture and killing the bacterium. Harmless to human cells, which lack cell walls, this selective toxicity makes it an ideal antibiotic.

Penicillin was initially difficult to isolate and purify. Development accelerated during World War II as a military necessity to treat infected wounds and prevent gangrene. Fleming's discovery arrived precisely when it was most needed. Mass production by fermentation in large tanks made penicillin widely available and affordable, transforming bacterial infection from often-fatal to treatable. By the war's end, millions of doses were produced monthly.

Penicillin exhibits a relatively broad spectrum of activity against gram-positive bacteria, though many bacteria subsequently evolved resistance through genetic mutations that altered cell wall precursor synthesis. It derives its name from the mold species that produces it, Penicillium notatum, which is now cultivated industrially for pharmaceutical production. Different strains of the mold produce varying quantities of penicillin.

Penicillin launched an entire field of antibiotic research, leading to the discovery of streptomycin, tetracycline, and countless other antimicrobial drugs. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this discovery that transformed medicine and saved untold millions of lives.
